💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that levent Alpöge states he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis.
  • “250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious,” Alpöge wrote.
  • The number came from a footnote in the four-page note he released with his Lean code on 20 November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that levent Alpöge states he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis. Now the Anthropic mathematician says the 250,000-page figure tied to his proof was a joke. He made the point late on Monday in a post on X headed “Stupid things I did”.

“250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious,” Alpöge wrote.

The number came from a footnote in the four-page note he released with his Lean code on 20 November. In it, he wrote that he had “amused” himself and “hit 250,000+ pages”. The note also said that posting such a text would be inappropriate, so he published only the code, as TNW reported on Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that the figure spread fast. The Register put it in its headline on Tuesday, calling the written proof “250,000 pages of slop”.

Alpöge said he had tried to signal the joke through the pedantry of the main theorem. His note described a Claude draft whose Theorem 1 opened by pointing out that the real numbers are totally ordered. But “people ran with it unfortunately”, he wrote.

When one X user joked that he had made the number up, he mentioned the pages were real:.

In a recent development, “No it wasn’t made up! But it would have been ridiculous to take that seriously as a real writeup is all,” he replied on X.

In the same thread, Alpöge said his Lean submission holds unnecessary material. Cleaning it up was harder than he expected, Aamir Khollam reported for Interesting Engineering. He also answered criticism of his write-up from mathematician Scott Armstrong, saying clear exposition has long been hard for him.

In a recent development, some readers took the thread to mean the proof was in doubt. A few hours later, he pushed back:.

According to recent reports, “People seem to be reading this as me saying there’s something wrong with the proof. I’m pretty confused. No? It literally checked out days ago?” Alpöge wrote on X.

Sources indicate that he was pointing to the checks of the code. On 21 November, the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative certified the proof as correct.

The Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1m for a proof, has moved the Riemann hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active”, The Register reported. It does not yet count it as solved.

Industry observers note that under Clay’s rules, a solution must appear in a qualifying outlet and stay open to scrutiny for at least two years. It also needs broad acceptance from mathematicians. Kevin Buzzard, of Imperial College London, has noted that nobody yet understands what the proof demonstrates.

Industry observers note that it is not the first time Alpöge has used X for a major result. In July, he posted there that Claude had found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds. Thanks to advances in active noise cancellation (ANC), they're great at keeping the noise of your commute at bay, and their in-ear design makes them super portable. But which should you buy?

At the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They've got the best ANC we've ever tested, and offer a comfortable fit so that you can wear them for long periods of time. There's little more we'd ask.

If they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. They don't cost anywhere near as much, but also offer great ANC and solid sound quality.

In a recent development, I maintain the site's buying guides for headphones, wireless earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, soundbars, and more. I have spent more than 20 years testing audio equipment for my own enjoyment, and was previously the Audio Editor here at Tom's Guide. There's nothing more I love than jamming out to my favorite tunes on audio equipment of different prices and sizes.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 bring improvements to the formula across the board, in all but one key area. If you were to unbox your brand-upcoming buds next to a pair of the old model, you'd be forgiven for wondering if you'd be shortchanged.

In a recent development, they look identical. All the way down to their eartip shape and silicone fitting wing, the QuietComfort Ultra Buds family is one that has a particular style that it has stuck with for a long time.

Pop them in your ears and you soon notice the difference. They've got even better ANC than the old model, with some of the most impressive noise canceling around. They block out everything — I took them on a long train journey, and found that all of the noise of my carriage was completely unnoticeable, even when not listening to music. It's like magic, as the orchestral sound swells and the noise disappears.

The transparency mode is very good as well, and it works well if you want to order your breakfast when you're going to work. The touch controls work well, and the charging case now contains a wireless charging coil so that you can more easily keep them fully charged.

Battery life is still not the best, though. Six hours with ANC on isn't quite up there, and four hours when you turn on 'immersive audio' is lackluster. It's not really worth turning the Immersive Audio setting on anyway.

It just thins out your music as it tries to distribute it around an artificially extended soundstage, and uses up an extra two hours of battery life. The soundstage is wide enough as it is, and the sound improved over the first model for some great audio as well.

They're still the best ANC buds you can get your hands on, and the Gen 2 just cemented their place in the annals of earbuds history. That ANC is just so good.

Industry observers note that with the AirPods Pro 3, Apple was looking to unseat Bose's buds from the top of the list. Unfortunately for Apple, Bose released the refreshed Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 just before the latest AirPods hit shelves, but the AirPods Pro 3 are still a significant step up over their predecessors.

According to recent reports, they've got sound to match the XM5, with a similarly natural sound profile and some extra juicy features that make them a whole lot more usable than the majority of the other options. They're a great jack of all trades and perfect for iPhone customers.

Industry observers note that the ANC is, Apple tells us, "2x as good as the AirPods Pro 2". In our testing, we've found that the ANC is, indeed, much better than the ANC of the previous models. It's better at blocking out sounds across the frequency spectrum, although it still focuses on the sounds you'll hear in your day-to-day life.

Sources indicate that that means that bus journeys are more comfortable and office stays more tolerable. The transparency mode is natural-sounding as well and gives you more battery life.

Industry observers note that there are some extra features on board the AirPods Pro 3. There's a heart rate monitor and Live Translation, although we found these to be novelty extras as opposed to 'reasons to buy.'.

There are meaningful improvements in some other key areas, however. Fit is far better, and it seals very well in the ear to help the ANC. The battery life is excellent, with 2 hours more than the previous model, bringing them up to par with the Sony earbuds.

There are a couple of drawbacks. Android users won't like their less impressive features for their OS, but you were probably eyeing up the buds from Sony and Bose. There's still only one color option — white — and I've got AirPods that have died permanently gray after spending too much time in my black jeans pocket.

The AirPods Pro 3 are still an excellent pair of buds for iPhone customers, however, and some of the best ANC buds around.

Industry observers note that there are good budget buds, but there are very few as impressive as the CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. If you weren’t already aware, CMF is Nothing's most affordable product range, and the 2A sit at the bottom price rung of the brand's earbud lineup.

You might have thought that such a low price would mean low-quality ANC — but no, that’s far from the truth. The CMF Buds (sorry CMF, I’m not typing “by Nothing” every time) 2A are a budget revelation when it comes to keeping unwanted noise at bay.

We found that the sound of buses and other public transport was blocked very well by the buds, making sure that your commute is more comfortable. It’s adaptive as well, changing and shifting depending on the ambient noise levels.

In a recent development, transparency mode was great when we wanted to order some lunch, with clear sound when we were chatting with the service staff. It’s not quite up there with the AirPods Pro 3 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but then you could buy nearly ten pairs of these for the same price as either of those.

They’re comfortable too, with loads of fitting options in the box so that you can dial them in according to your specific fitting preferences. The battery life is solid with 35 hours on tap — that’s plenty to get you through a week's worth of work and commuting. Multi-point makes sure you can connect to different devices without the need to dip into the settings menu, and it works well.

They’re obviously not perfect — some compromises have been made to keep the price down. They feel a bit cheap, and there’s no auto-pause when you take them in and out of your ears. But again, when you consider the price, the few cons are very easy to forgive.

Recent findings suggest that sound is impressive, and there are loads of extra features in the Nothing X app like a customizable EQ. We love the CMF Buds 2A, and we think you will too once you’ve got the $30 wonders in your pocket — and you want to keep the noise of your busy 7:30 AM train at bay.

In a recent development, sony has been trying to take the ANC fight to Bose since the latter released its finest, and sometimes Sony has come out on top. In this case, though, it’s the runner-up — but it's so close. There are still key reasons to pick up the WF-1000XM6 instead of the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.

But about that ANC; it’s very good. We tested the buds in a range of different environments, from the office, a train, a busy city, and more. The noise cancellation kept out just about everything, and didn’t affect the sound of the music we were listening to.

It loses out to the QuietComfort in the smoothness of the delivery. That means that changes in environments are handled slightly more roughly than Boses pair, with a little noise leaking in before the algorithm takes notice. To be clear — it’s so close. If you don’t try both, you won’t notice. Side by side though, there is an edge to the Sony that’s not present in the Bose buds.

Recent findings suggest that the sound, though, is better than Bose’s buds. There’s more delicacy up top, and they’re less low-end heavy. Sony’s tuning is more pleasing to our ears across a range of different genres, making them a better bet for the sound-quality-conscious. The AirPods Pro 3 sound even better, though.

They’re comfortable too, with a solid range of different tips for different ear shapes. The buds themselves a slightly strange shape, and the case is a dumb shape (it's covered with angles, so it’s less comfortable to fit in a pocket than the lovely smooth Bose and Apple options), but this is still a stylish and comfy pair of wireless earbuds.

Battery life is… fine. It’s unimproved from the previous model, the WF-1000XM5, with around 8 hours of use with ANC turned on. That’s more than the Bose buds and around the same as the AirPods Pro 3. Still, we’d like to see more battery life from flagship earbuds, considering how much you get with more budget buds.

Industry observers note that so in the end, it all comes down to a couple of things. If you want the best noise canceling, buy the Bose earbuds. If you want something with great ANC that works with an iPhone, then get the AirPods Pro 3. If you want something that works well with everything, offers great ANC and excellent sound quality, then pick the Sony WF-1000XM6.

According to recent reports, the Noble Fokus Amadeus bring a certain class to proceedings. They're covered in a very regal red colorway, and the buds themselves have a resin finish that makes them look almost like jewelry. And I love them.

Sources indicate that they're super comfortable, especially if you use the flanged eartips. Those will also make your ANC better, and it was already really good. It blocked out the fan in my office, and makes bus journeys and train trips a whole lot more tolerable. It's not quite up there with the Bose ANC, but it does get close to the Sony XM series. That's impressive, especially given that Noble is a much smaller organization.

The sound is the best bit, though. Slip them into your ears, and you're treated to the very best audio experience this side of $400. The highs are incredibly detailed, the mids are incredible, and the bass is impactful. They sound excellent — hence why they're on the list.

They lack some of the features of the competition, like the Spatial Audio of the AirPods and 360 reality audio you'll find on Sony buds, but they more than make up for it thanks to their incredible sound.

For audiophiles looking for their portable audio fix, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are the buds for you.

Fitness buds are a dime a dozen, with plenty of options available should you want to listen to music while you work out. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the latest buds from Apple's subsidiary, and they also happen to be the best buds for fitness fanatics. They've got a useful fitting hook on each bud, and then heart rate monitors to make sure they stay in place.

Recent findings suggest that the noise canceling, as you'd hope, is excellent. I found it perfect for most different settings, be that a quiet office or a bustling train. I'm not known for my exercise, however, so I spoke to someone who is — and what they thought of the noise canceling on board.

They took them for months of long running sessions and other fitness work, and found they blocked noise very well. Gyms silenced, annoying traffic brought to nothing. If you want to make sure your jogs, cycling, or even your swimming is distraction-free, then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the buds for you.

I was also very impressed with the battery life of the buds. According to Beats, there are 10 hours of ANC on battery life out of the buds, and my testing proved that to be pretty much spot on. That extends to 45 hours when you put them back in the (very large) charging case, for some of the best battery life in the segment. It will depend on volume level and even genre, but expect good staying power.

According to recent reports, sound does trip up slightly. They've got plenty of detail and some fairly dynamic bass, but there's an unfortunate cut-off in the lower mids that takes some of the edge out of your music. For most people, it's not going to be a problem. But if you're picky about how your music sounds, you may be better off with a different pair of earbuds.

In a recent development, the heart rate monitor is useful if you want to track more of your fitness metrics, but we found that it wasn't the most accurate. Not a massive issue, but one worth noting.

In the end, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a solid ANC option for everyone, but they're particularly good for those looking for a fitness companion.

It has been revealed that samsung’s buds have never topped best lists, but they’ve always had a space reserved. While they might not have the same “all things for all people” vibes as the Sony WF-1000XM6, the ultra-impressive noise canceling of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, or the Apple user features of the AirPods line, there has been little better for people of Samsung’s phones than Samsung’s buds. They offer great performance at a slightly lower price and bring some exclusive features to the table, making them even better.

Sources indicate that noise-canceling-wise, you’re looking at performance that gets close to the AirPods and the Sony buds, just slotting in behind the QuietComfort Ultra. They do a great job of keeping noise at bay, as we discovered when we put them head-to-head with the Bose buds, and with music playing, you won’t find any horrible noises making their way through.

Recent findings suggest that transparency mode is similarly excellent, and doesn’t add the same robotic hue as cheaper buds. Perfect for when you need to speak to someone and don’t want to pop your earbuds out. In case you lose them. The algorithms that Samsung uses here are very good, and there are different levels you can access with the Samsung settings app and a separate Samsung earbuds application you can install.

Industry observers note that sound-wise, they’re very good as well, bringing plenty of bass and richness to the table. They’re a “big” sounding earbud, with plenty of depth. They’re similarly lovely in the mids department, making sure that music sounds great no matter the genre. Detail heads will miss out on some of the really high and clear stuff, but they’ll be better served by the buds from Sony. Either way, the sound is top-notch, even if it does focus on different parts of the frequency range.

Battery life is solid as a rock, although not quite as special as the likes of the Apple or Sony buds. Seven hours of staying power is plenty to get you through the work day, especially if you charge them in the case over your lunch break. The 30 hours of life in the case is actually better than the competition, which is always good, and makes sure they’re not going to need a wall outlet as often.

AI features are going to be useful for some and less so for others. Still, the likes of Interpreter and others are fun extras, even if you do have to have a Samsung device for them to work properly. If you’re looking for the perfect accompaniment to your S23 or newer, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are the way to go.

Wired earbuds are back, and there’s no bigger sign than Bose’s noise-canceling version of the format. It’s not the first time that Bose has made wired earbuds with ANC inside, but this version brings the latest algorithms to the table for excellent ANC performance paired with a reliable, tethered connection. They’re good to, although it seems that Bose is keeping some stuff back for either the more expensive wired option or to account for a lack of a dedicated power source for the mics and tech needed for ANC.

In a recent development, the ANC is good. Very good, in fact — we found that it blocked plenty of noise when walking down a street or working in a busy office. If you’ve not experienced the likes of the upper ANC echelons, these are going to be perfectly serviceable for everyday use. They’re just a little weaker than some of the other options on this list, with some higher sounds making their way through the barrier.

It has been revealed that transparency works well enough, making sure that you can hear what's going on the other side of the buds without all the extra noise around you. It does affect the sound of the buds slightly, however, so you’ll pay the price in sound quality when you’re ordering your McDonald's breakfast. The price you pay for a double sausage and egg McMuffin, one supposes.

The sound quality is a highlight of the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds. The bass is less in your face than prior models, although it’s a lovely addition to the table. Similarly, high-range and lower-register mids sound great no matter the genre you’re listening to. It's a less in-your-face audio experience than previous Bose products, which is a nice change.

Sources indicate that then there’s the wire, which comes with both pros and cons. You don’t have to worry about battery life, for one. The power for the ANC is pulled straight from your phone or laptops battery, so your earbuds will only die when your listening device does. That’s good. You also get lossless audio thanks to the USB-C connection, and low-latency listening should you want to play games or watch movies and TV shows on the go without the sound getting behind what’s going on on-screen.

The bad thing? You’re tethered. Forget to unplug them or take them out when you stand up and you’ll send your phone flying across the floor or violently disconnect them from your laptop. You’ll need to get used to it, that’s for sure. But for under $100? It’s well worth the trade-off, if not only for effectively unlimited battery life.

Recent findings suggest that we test a lot of noise-canceling earbuds, but not everything can make it into our buying guides. Whether that's down to better performance or stronger features from rival models in a particular category and price, some miss ranking in this list by the slightest of margins. With that in mind, these models are strong contenders and great alternative considerations.

Apple's upcoming noise-canceling earbuds are here, and they land at a lower price than the previous model. We were impressed with the ANC this time around, although the battery life simply isn't good enough to kick it with the options above. Still, Apple people on a budget will find a lot to like here.

The ZE300 are Final’s lightest earbuds yet, and they’re perhaps some of the most comfortable buds out there right now. For less than $50, you’re getting excellent sound quality across many genres and highly effective ANC indoors, packaged into a pressure-relieving design with a comfortable fit.

Read our full Final ZE300 review.

It has been revealed that A strong pair of cheap wireless noise-canceling earbuds, the EarFun Pro 3 deliver nearly 40 hours of listening (with their case), making them some of the longest-lasting among their peers like the Soundcore Liberty 4 NC. The ANC in the EarFun set is effective and the buds also support aptX Adaptive audio, and have a custom equalizer in its app. Our review also mentioned the good call quality and wireless charging.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 3 review.

Soundcore has finally joined the big leagues, although the Liberty 5 Pro Max aren't quite up there with the best yet. They sound good and offer some useful features, but we'd say you're still better off with the buds from Sony, Apple and Bose right now.

Read our full Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

We've judged the best noise-canceling earbuds on several factors: audio performance, battery life, Bluetooth range, call quality, comfort and fit, and the effectiveness of the noise cancellation. We also weigh special features, such as included apps, and how easy they are to use.

During the testing phase, our reviewers wear each pair of earbuds for 2 hours at a time throughout the course of a week, to test comfort over time.

Industry observers note that ANC, meanwhile, is tested in both indoor and outdoor environments where ambient sounds are produced at high levels. This includes airplanes, city parks, convenience shops, offices, and public transportation. ANC earbuds programmed with transparency modes are also tested thoroughly to determine how well the listener can hear their surroundings.

For sound quality, we listen to many different sample tracks and span as many music genres as possible, including hip-hop, rock, jazz, classical and R&B, while evaluating volume, clarity, and fullness. Find out what we listen for during our testing process and how to get the best headphone sound for you.

And now that more streaming music services are offering high-resolution audio, be sure to read our audio codec FAQ for all you need to know.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we’ll rate noise-canceling earbuds on our five-point system, with 1 being the worst and 5 the best. If a pair is particularly excellent, with a robust range of qualities, we may award it an Editor's Choice badge.

The first item to check off the list when shopping for the best noise-canceling earbuds is their active noise cancellation performance, which shouldn’t be confused with passive noise cancellation. What are the differences?

In a recent development, 1. Active vs. passive noise cancellation: ANC uses advanced circuitry and microphones to pick up noise signals and create inverse waves that cancel out these sonic disruptions, whereas PNC physically isolates high-pitched sounds through the headphone design and materials. Most headphones advertised with noise cancellation are categorized under ANC.

2. Battery life: Noise-canceling earbuds have a reputation for sucking up lots of power, so you’ll want a pair that holds a charge long enough to get you through a long business flight or weekly commutes. Noise-canceling wireless earbuds are usually rated for 4.5 to 8 hours, but with included charging cases the total possible playback time might be much more competitive.

Think about how long and how often you’d want to wear your earbuds for on lengthy trips. A longer “per charge” battery life is better, but if you only want some entertainment on short commutes then it not quite so vital, as you’ll probably be storing the buds in their case more regularly.

3. Sound quality: ANC technology can compress sound and reduce dynamics, which may affect audio performance when turned on. In some cases, you’ll notice a background hiss when listening to music. However, the best noise-canceling earbuds limit these disruptions to deliver full, crisp sound.

4. Design: The look, build and feel of a pair of in-ear 'buds is massively important when selecting the best noise-canceling earbuds, so consider how they look and feel and whether the style is right for you. In our best noise-canceling headphones round up we mention that over-ear headphones tend to give the best noise cancellation, but some of the more recent wireless in-ear models are proving to be just as effective.

Sources indicate that 5. Pricing considerations: Obviously, price is a big consideration when looking for the best noise-canceling earbuds. Although there are always exceptions, big-name brands will typically command a bit extra, but generally speaking, the less you spend on a pair of headphones the greater the chance that sound and features will be compromised. Going for a budget option isn't always the best choice, as any money you save on your purchase won't do you much good if you're constantly needing to recharge your audio gear, or the sound quality is poor.

Industry observers note that ANC explained: Active noise cancellation (ANC) models employ built-in mics to pick up ambient sounds around the wearer. An identical but inverted audio signal of the noise is played back to the listener through the headphones.

In a recent development, listeners aren't aware of this happening of course, as the inverted (or out of phase) signal effectively 'cancels out' the noise of the surroundings for the headphone wearer. The process removes the external sounds, which results in a significant reduction in the level of background noise at the very least.

Given that it uses both more computational power and a bunch of microphones in order to work, ANC has an effect on your battery life. This often chops a couple of hours off, so they won't last quite as long. If you want to keep the battery going for longer then you'll want to keep the noise canceling turned off.

According to recent reports, in most cases, noise-canceling earbuds are very effective at reducing ambient sounds. There are limits, though, and some designs are less effective at silencing certain types of sounds than others.

The process is fast but it can’t physically occur in real time, so active noise cancellation (ANC) works best with consistent low-frequency sounds as opposed to higher-pitched, inconsistent sounds like human speech.

Vehicle engines and droning air conditioners are easy to cancel out, but the shorter wavelength of high-frequency sounds, like a sudden blast from a car horn, makes it tougher for the ANC’s anti-noise waves to perfectly mask these bursts.

Even so, all sounds will be at least a little quieter when you’re wearing noise-canceling headphones, and many sounds can be completely silenced even on low-cost pairs or earbuds.

Andreas Kling — Mon, 23 Nov 2026.

Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^).

Ladybird is a browser with a fresh engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

Sources indicate that we want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves rapidly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

It has been revealed that if you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

In a recent development, openAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The firm also set a retirement date for two older models.

OpenAI says it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

If you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise consumers.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI claims it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

One of football’s largest financial lenders abandoned a planned £1.5billion loan to Manchester City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

The decision by US private capital group Apollo Global Management is the latest evidence that the money markets deem City a financial risk, as the club prepare an appeal against their conviction on the vast majority of 115 Premier League charges of inflating income through sham contracts.

It has been revealed that it was reported by Bloomberg last week that a German lender, Oldenburgische Landesbank (OL), had pulled out of a deal that would have let Brazilian top-flight side Palmeiras take a large upfront payment against instalments City are due to pay them for midfielder Allan Elias, signed this summer for £32million with £2m add-ons. That bank views City as a reputational and financial risk.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Apollo was in the final stages of negotiating the loan to City Football Group (CFG) in September, when the deal collapsed after the ruling that they artificially inflated their financial position to the tune of more than £900m over nine years.

City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan injected £100m into the club in the month after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Mansour, who has only been present at one City home game since Abu Dhabi bought the club in 2008, has made no public comment on the club’s conviction, which delivers huge reputational damage to his image-conscious country.

In a recent development, there are signs that football is preparing for a strong legal attack from Abu Dhabi if City lose their appeal. Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors in the event of sponsors Etihad and Etisalat suing them, it was also unveiled on Thursday. Legal indemnity will be in place for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittain and three other non-executive directors.

US private capital group Apollo Global Management abandoned a £1.5billion loan to Man City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

City owner Sheikh Mansou injected £100m into the club after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi.

But the refusal of credit by Apollo, which has loaned £80m to Premier League football club Nottingham Forest and has a minority stake in Championship side Wrexham, demonstrates that the capital markets think City are imperilled, with the appeal process by no means straightforward.

If an appeal failed, City could seek a judicial review of the commission's findings at the High Court. But to do so, they would need to demonstrate that the Premier League acted outside its powers or reached a conclusion which no reasonable authority could have reached. City would need the High Court’s permission to make a judicial review application and the bar is high.

Recent findings suggest that financial analyst Paul Quinn wrote on The Esk website that Apollo’s issue had been with City, not Abu Dhabi itself. Three weeks ago, Apollo agreed to take a minority stake in Mubadala Capital, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund chaired by Sheikh Mansour and run by City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak. Apollo and City have not commented.

Quinn said that CFG needed the money because it was not self-funding, despite City’s financial strength. CFG’s pre-tax loss widened from £122.2m to £292.3m in the last financial year. City produced £694.1m of CFG’s £888m group revenue and ran up a £9m loss.

#176929. How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D)

How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years.
  • This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s Mechanical Watch page.
  • You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the side; on a phone, drag sideways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years. Many of their core parts were invented even earlier for giant cathedral tower clocks before being shrunk into portable timepieces. This page explains how a modern one works. I personally think it’s fascinating that a well-calibrated, purely mechanical device can keep time with 99.99% accuracy for $100. They also changed the world and look good on your wrist.

This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s Mechanical Watch page. You can think of this page as a simpler introduction or background. When you’re finished with this, that page gives more depth.

You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the side; on a phone, drag sideways.

Start with the part that keeps time. In 1675 Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, invented the hairspring. It is a flat spiral of steel ribbon, finer than a hair. Its outer end is held still, and its inner end is free to turn. Twist the inner end and let go, and the spiral winds and unwinds, back and forth, at a steady rate. In this drawing it swings once every two seconds, and the rest of the watch follows that beat.

It has been revealed that why does a spring swing? Think of a diving board. Bend it down, and it pushes back: an elastic restoring force. Let go, and it does not stop at straight. It overshoots, bends the other way, and comes back again: it oscillates. With no friction, it would oscillate forever.

It has been revealed that A hairspring is a diving board rolled up. The board’s rest shape is a straight line; the hairspring’s is a spiral. Take hold of the slider under the next picture, and drag it to the right.

Recent findings suggest that “Bend” becomes “wind”, and “straight” becomes “rest”. Now give the hairspring a twist: drag the slider to wind the spiral away from its rest shape, and let go.

It pushes back. It overshoots and swings, just as the board did. This one move is the whole idea of the hairspring.

The hairspring is only half of the timekeeper. The other half is the balance wheel. While most of its mass is around the outside, it is actually fixed to the spring’s inner end. The spring provides the restoring force. The wheel provides the mass and inertia.

According to recent reports, A hairspring alone would oscillate far too fast to count. The wheel slows it to a pace that the gears can count.

Mass also makes the swing steady. Push an empty playground swing, and it jerks about. Put a child on it and it swings much more gracefully. A heavy wheel carries its own momentum, so a knock to your wrist, or turning it upside down, barely changes its rhythm.

How good is it? A well-calibrated mechanical watch, even an everyday Seiko or Citizen, is about 99.99% accurate. A day has 86,400 seconds, so that watch gains or loses about nine seconds a day.

According to recent reports, I’m not particularly handy with mechanical things. If I tried to build a table it would wobble because things would be off by a few percent. So it kind of blows my mind that, for $100, I can get a simple, everyday, purely mechanical system and tweak it to be 99.99% accurate!

Sources indicate that A second hand that just moves back and forth isn’t very useful. We need it to turn one way only. The escapement turns the swing into steps.

The escape wheel is being turned by a mechanism we’ll explain soon, so it’s hidden on this diagram. Without something to stop it, it would just turn and turn.

Recent findings suggest that its two prongs (called stones) stick in the wheel’s teeth: a tooth lands on a stone, and the wheel stops. Each time the fork rocks, one stone lets a tooth go, and the other stone catches the next tooth. The tooth escapes, and that is where the name comes from.

What rocks the fork? The balance does. On its staff is a small impulse jewel, which sits in the notch at the end of the fork. It’s actually a synthetic ruby or sapphire, so it really is a jewel, a precious stone.

In a recent development, as the balance swings through the middle, the jewel strikes the fork and flips it one way. On the swing back, it flips it the other way.

In a recent development, so, at each swing, the balance lets the wheel take one small step. The step ends when the next tooth lands on a stone, hard enough to make a sound. This is the tick and the tock of a watch.

Before we go on, something that trips people up until they think it through. How long does the second hand take to go once around the dial?

According to recent reports, each tick is one second, and sixty ticks brings it all the way around. So the second hand makes a complete circle once a minute. A hand is named for what it counts, not for how long it takes to make a full 360° turn.

The escapement gets the escape wheel turning at a precise rate. But the second hand must turn once a minute, and the escape wheel turns faster than that. To convert a faster rotation into a slower one, a watch uses gears: a small gear that meshes with a massive one.

Industry observers note that the teeth on the two gears must have the same spacing, so they mesh neatly. Each tooth fits in a gap of the other gear, so the teeth go past each other one for one, and both rims move at the same speed. Four teeth on each gear are colored. Those four teeth are half of the small gear, but only a quarter of the big one. So the small gear turns twice for each turn of the big one: twice the circumference, half the speed.

Now attach the smaller gear (called a pinion) to the escape wheel. The gears do not spin freely any more: they move on one tick at a time, with the escape wheel. The escapement controls the speed of the whole train of gears.

Sources indicate that the big gear pushing the small gear (pinion) is the force turning the escape wheel. What turns the big wheel? That’s a mechanism we’ll explain soon.

It has been revealed that in this watch, the big gear (called the fourth wheel) turns exactly once a minute: just what the second hand needs! So the second hand goes on the big gear’s axle. It is the first part of the watch that we can read.

According to recent reports, the second hand turns once a minute. The minute hand must turn once an hour: sixty times slower. So we could try the same trick, and have a gear that’s 60 times bigger than the small gear.

According to recent reports, but there’s a limit to how small you can manufacture the small gear, so the major gear would be huge. And it would have a lot of teeth which adds to the cost. Plus, it would turn the wrong way, counterclockwise, because every gear turns the opposite direction from the one it meshes with.

Recent findings suggest that so the watch slows in two stages. The third wheel runs 7½ times slower, and the center wheel runs 8 times slower than that.

7½ times 8 is 60, so the center wheel turns once an hour.

Industry observers note that the minute hand goes on the center wheel’s axle (arbor), in the middle of the dial. It makes a full turn once an hour.

Industry observers note that the center wheel pushes the third wheel which pushes the fourth wheel which pushes the escape wheel. Next up, the mechanism that pushes the center wheel and powers the whole watch.

Sources indicate that this is a spiral spring, like the hairspring. But instead of swinging back and forth, it does one slow unwind over a day or two. In the illustration above, it’s at rest.

Industry observers note that below, the outer end is held in place. Drag the slider to wind it up. The spring keeps its length, so its coils draw in toward the center.

In a recent development, when wound away from its rest shape, the dashed line, it pushes back, as the hairspring does. A tiny one-way ratchet locks the axle (arbor) so it can only turn one way. To unwind the mainspring, let go of the outer end by pressing the button.

The block is gone, and the outer end swings around until the spring lies on its rest shape again. That fling is the energy that the winding put in.

A watch harnesses that force by attaching the spring’s outer end to a toothed drum called the barrel, invented by Jean-Antoine Lépine around 1760.

As the mainspring pushes the barrel, the barrel’s teeth drive the gear train we just built. This is the “hidden mechanism” we mentioned earlier.

Because the ratchet stops the arbor from turning backwards, the spring has only one way to unwind: by its outer end turning the barrel. Press the button under the figure, and six hours pass in six seconds. The barrel turns once, the minute hand six times, and the coils move back out to the wall. When the spring is completely unwound, the watch stops.

In a recent development, the hour hand must turn twice a day. That’s once every twelve hours. Unlike the 60:1, a 12:1 gear is doable.

In a recent development, but the hour hand on that wheel’s axle (arbor) is off center! And it would run backward (counterclockwise): a pair of meshing gears turn opposite directions.

So we use the same two-step trick we used for the minute hand. This time, 3:1 going out and 4:1 coming back. 3:1 × 4:1 = 12:1.

The hour hand goes on the hour wheel, in the middle, under the minute hand, attached to a hollow tube (pipe) that slips over the minute hand’s axle. It turns clockwise, twice a day.

And that’s how a mechanical watch works!

Here’s a recap, retracing our steps in reverse, from the hour hand to the hairspring. The tour plays by itself, like a short film. The time scale in the corner says how much faster than real time each segment runs.

The hour hand is driven by a pair of gears totaling 12:1.

Sources indicate that this feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:.

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

It has been revealed that iPhone owners with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

Recent findings suggest that this one isn’t really a newly introduced feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quad9

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French consumers.
  • We are unhappy to have reached this impasse.
  • We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder manufacturer) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French consumers. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond rapidly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.

We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.

We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder manufacturer) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Right now, the courts have upheld beInâs demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.

Sources indicate that we have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.

Industry observers note that this is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: consumers who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world.

Industry observers note that there is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French users” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated.

Our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French consumers is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist.Â.

These geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly, IP location does not necessarily equate to user location, geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their consumers in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is nothing about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself.

According to recent reports, the data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have.

We could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French customers from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us.Â.

By accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem - it is not. We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.

So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French people but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

Quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end users, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on all our service addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition.

We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start âthe beginning of the endâ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end customers are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user.Â.

It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant.

Industry observers note that we have seen recent articles about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet.

This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually won in Germany; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have said we will deliver to owners worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys.Â.

Industry observers note that legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fightâand keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider donating or becoming a sponsor today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, xiaomi’s revenue fell for a third quarter in a row as rising memory prices squeezed its phones and its car sales slowed.
  • Recent findings suggest that profit fell faster.
  • Xiaomi said it kept raising its spending on AI, and described the quarter’s conditions in the filing:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xiaomi’s Smart Factory in Beijing.

According to recent reports, xiaomi’s revenue fell for a third quarter in a row as rising memory prices squeezed its phones and its car sales slowed. Revenue dropped 5.2% to 107.2 billion yuan ($16.1bn) in the three months to September. The manufacturer reported the figures in its results filing on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that profit fell faster. Net profit dropped 68.4% to 3.9 billion yuan. Adjusted net profit, a non-IFRS measure, fell 56.8% to 4.9 billion yuan. Gross margin slipped to 20.2%, from 22.9% a year earlier.

Xiaomi said it kept raising its spending on AI, and described the quarter’s conditions in the filing:.

“The costs of key components, including memory, continued to rise and industry competition further intensified,” Xiaomi wrote.

Recent findings suggest that xiaomi shipped 30.7 million smartphones, down 29.1% from 43.3 million a year earlier. It remarked it cut shipments of low-end phones on purpose. Global smartphone shipments fell 20% in the quarter, according to Omdia data cited by Xiaomi.

Sources indicate that the average selling price rose 39.8% to a record 1,486 yuan. That offset most of the drop, and phone revenue fell 0.8%, to 45.6 billion yuan. The phone gross margin fell to 9.2%, from 11.1%, which Xiaomi put down mainly to higher component prices. Its Xiaomi 18 Fold, launched in September from 10,999 yuan, runs on the tech giant’s own Xring O3 chip.

In a recent development, company president Lu Weibing stated on the earnings call that memory prices would likely stay high through the first half of 2027. Peggy Ye and Howard Liu reported his comments for the South China Morning Post.

Sources indicate that the unit that now covers cars, AI and other new businesses saw revenue fall 17.7%, to 23.9 billion yuan. Car revenue alone dropped 19.9%, to 22.7 billion yuan. Xiaomi delivered 100,975 vehicles, down 7% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported. China’s passenger car retail market shrank 24% in the period, the filing mentioned.

The unit posted an operating loss of 3.4 billion yuan. Executives put it down to growing investment in AI, according to Bloomberg. The filing also blamed fewer deliveries of the high-end SU7 Ultra for a lower margin.

It has been revealed that xiaomi pointed to its new SkyNomad range of extended-range SUVs, priced from 209,900 yuan. It stated orders passed 70,000 in the first month of sales. Deliveries in the quarter included more than 10,000 SkyNomads.

Recent findings suggest that on the call, executives kept the blueprint to enter Germany in the third quarter of 2027, Bloomberg reported. They said recent EU trade barriers would not greatly change its strategy for Europe. Xiaomi has signed agreements with eight German dealer groups.

Research and development costs reached 9.2 billion yuan in the quarter. Over nine months they rose 16.5%, to 27.4 billion yuan. In September, Xiaomi released its MiMo-V2.6 models as open source. It also revealed the design behind its next model, MiMo-V3.

It has been revealed that the results follow a second-quarter profit drop in August. Xiaomi has also bought back about 431.5 million of its own shares this year, worth about HK$13.1bn.

#176925. Tech Report: I’ve been testing the Coros Vertix 4 for 5 days — here’s what I like and dislike about the Garmin Fenix rival so far

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1493 w)

Tech Report: I’ve been testing the Coros Vertix 4 for 5 days — here’s what I like and dislike about the Garmin Fenix rival so far

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.
  • I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.
  • You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.

I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs. For those wondering why Coros went from 2S to 4, skipping a Vertix 3, it’s to bring the Vertix 4 into line with its other watches: the Coros Apex 4 and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

The Coros Vertix 4 debuted on 24 November 2026 and will be available to order from 27 November. It costs $799 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., a $100/£70 price rise on the Vertix 2S.

It does come in significantly cheaper than the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, though, which starts at $999. However, there are some rivals that come in cheaper than the Vertix 4, with the Suunto Vertical 2 titanium model, costing $699/£639, and older Garmin Fenix models appearing in sales — the Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon right now, for example.

The Vertix has previously had a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, and while that does have some advantages, most notably longer battery life, I much prefer the AMOLED display on the Vertix 4.

It’s a very big, bright screen and easier to read than the MIP display on the Vertix 2S in all conditions I find, even in bright sunlight.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The latest satellite maps also look great on the display, and the battery life on the Vertix 4 is still very good.

While it would have been great for Coros to make the Vertix 4 available with both MIP and AMOLED options, as Garmin does with the Fenix, it’s perhaps not practical in production terms, and I do think AMOLED is the better option here, with the Apex 4 offering a MIP alternative in the Coros line-up.

Adventure watches are, by design, big and bold devices to strap to your wrist, but the Vertix 2S was a little too huge, and the Coros Vertix 4 is a much more enjoyable watch to wear all day.

It’s thinner and lighter than its predecessor while having a larger display, and doesn’t feel too bulky even on my slim wrist.

In the past, I think Coros watches could be accused of prioritizing substance over style, which is no bad thing, but it’s better to have both, and both of the brand’s 2026 rolls out — the Pace 4 Pro and now Vertix 4 — have been more attractive than past options.

Ever since Garmin added a built-in flashlight to the Fenix 7X, it’s been a feature that people have wanted in their smartwatch, and the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get it.

Coros has swerved from the usual flashlight setup used by other brands, though, sticking its light on the side of the Vertix 4, between the digital dial and back button, as opposed to on the top as Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit do.

This has its advantages — the flashlight naturally focuses the way your arm is pointing, and you can switch the orientation of the buttons on the watch if you wear it on your right wrist.

I’m still on the fence about whether I prefer this or having the flashlight on top of the watch, but ultimately it’s a big addition to the Vertix line in general, and a very handy feature to have.

It has been revealed that another interesting upcoming feature on the Vertix 4 is satellite maps, which you can download to the watch and use instead of the standard maps. This is a feature I’m testing in beta, with it expected to launch in early 2027.

The satellite maps look great on the AMOLED display, and at times, it's a bit clearer to see what’s around you using them, especially in the forest.

It was pretty quick and easy to get my local area onto the watch through the Coros app, though the satellite map files are larger than the standard, so you will want to be choosy with the areas you download to the watch.

While the standard maps on the watch work fine, having the satellite option is useful at times, and it differentiates the Vertix 4 from other brands since these maps are free.

The Vertix 2S offers incredible battery life — it lasted me 22 days on a charge and even outperformed the Garmin Enduro 2 on this front.

Given the switch to an AMOLED display, the fear would be that the Vertix 4 fell short on this front in comparison, but the listed stats are still very impressive for the watch.

Coros suggests it will last up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on, and it offers 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on.

So far, the Vertix is on track to beat those estimates for me, although aided by the fact that I haven't used it for sleep tracking so far.

With the screen always on and running every day using the most accurate multi-band mode, it’s on track to last over 10 days.

All the Coros watches rolled out over the past couple of years have impressed me with their GPS accuracy, and that’s the case with the Vertix 4 so far as well.

I’ve been running with it and the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, with both set to their most accurate mode, and checking the GPS tracks afterwards. The Vertix 4 tracks have been spot on and in line with the Fenix 9 Pro on pace and distance stats throughout the runs too.

Unlike GPS accuracy, the heart rate accuracy of the Vertix 4 has been a bit iffy in my early testing when comparing the readings to a chest strap.

In the Vertix 4’s defence, I’ve been testing it in cold weather, when optical sensors on watches do tend to be less accurate, but I’ve still been a little underwhelmed by the results.

Sources indicate that on my easy runs, it’s mostly been pretty close to a chest strap, but on a hard progression run, the Vertix 4’s readings were too high throughout. Based on my early tests, you’d definitely be wise to pair a chest strap to the Vertix 4, at least in cold conditions.

The Vertix 4 is noticeably slimmer and lighter than past versions, but it’s still quite a major watch, and Coros does not offer any size options, something that Garmin does with the Fenix 9.

There are the Apex 4 and Pace 4 Pro as smaller alternatives in the Coros line-up, but if you want the flagship model, you have to accept that it only comes in one size, and it’s a biggie.

It doesn’t take long when testing a Coros watch to realize that they really make sports watches, not smartwatches.

The Vertix 4 can store music, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch; it doesn’t pair with streaming services. It also doesn’t offer NFC payments, and you can’t customize the watch face as much as on rivals.

Personally, I don’t miss these smart features much, but they are a selling point not only true smartwatches like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but also Garmin watches, which combine great sports tracking with useful smarts.

#176924. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4745 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon confirmed his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Recent findings suggest that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is notable because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

According to recent reports, RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

It has been revealed that recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The manufacturer’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company unveiled a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

Recent findings suggest that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Industry observers note that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
